Where it began

Quinton de Kock was born in Johannesburg on 17 December 1992 and went to King Edward VII School, where he stood out early and played for the Old Eds club. He was only 16 when he first played for Gauteng's senior side in 2009–10.

At the Under-19 World Cup in 2012 he made 126 from 106 balls against Namibia and finished the tournament with 284 runs, while keeping wicket neatly as well. Within a year he was playing for South Africa.

The player

His first international game was a Twenty20 match against New Zealand in December 2012, when he took the gloves so AB de Villiers could have a rest. His Test debut followed in February 2014 against Australia at Port Elizabeth, where he played purely as a batter. His first Test hundred, 129 not out against England in 2016, came from number seven.

He played 54 Tests from 2014 to 2021 and made 3,300 runs at 38.82, with 6 hundreds and a best of 141 not out against the West Indies in 2021. Behind the stumps he held 221 catches and made 11 stumpings, and he was the quickest keeper, by matches played, to reach both 150 and 200 Test dismissals. He led South Africa in four Tests and won two, and he stepped away from Test cricket at the end of 2021.

What made him special

He loved to attack from the first ball. In December 2013 he made three one-day hundreds in a row against India, and at the 2023 World Cup he made four hundreds, including 174 against Bangladesh. Bowlers who pitched short tended to regret it, and quickly.

His first World Cup, in 2015, brought fewer runs than he would have liked. He made up for it with interest eight years later.

Away from the middle

Cricket South Africa named him its Cricketer of the Year in 2017, and again its Men's Cricketer of the Year in 2020. He was Mumbai Indians' leading run-scorer when they won the IPL in 2019, and he has played franchise cricket all over the world, from England's Hundred to Australia's Big Bash.

After leaving Tests he carried on in the shorter formats. He helped South Africa reach their first T20 World Cup final in 2024, and in 2025 he came back to one-day cricket and was named player of the series on his return in Pakistan.

And finally

For a man who spent his days crouching patiently behind the stumps, he was never one to dawdle with the bat. In 2023 he reached a T20 international fifty in 15 balls, the fastest by a South African. Keepers are supposed to be the calm ones; nobody seems to have told him.
